en: — *Sthitisamāsa* (The Compendium on Abiding).
Toh. no. 2227. Derge Tanjur, vol. WI, folios 92r.6–99v.5.
*Sahajavajra*, the disciple of Mātṛpāda (Maitrīgupta).
Translated by Dhiriśrījñāna and Rma ban Chos ’bar. Revised by Bar ston, Bla ma Rgya gar ba, and Mtshur Lo tsā ba.

DM: – I suppose the Bar ston mentioned here [in the colophon] might possibly be Bar ston Rdo rje rgyal mtshan (simply because he is the only Bar ston I am aware of). – A Sanskrit manuscript has been preserved in Nepal (information from Isabelle Onians’ dissertation). – Some translations as well? – *Phyag chen khrid mdzod*, vol. 1, pp. 358–378.
— *Drepung Catalog*, p. 1713. Here, the title is *Gnas bsdus pa*. NAK 5/139 = NGMPP B 24/4 [not 324/4 as in Iwata!].

Folio 13 — 116–126a [Vajrayāna Section] Folio 15 — 136cd–146d [Vajrayāna Section] Folio 19 — 172b–179 + colophon [Vajrayāna Section]

Perhaps another manuscript? NAK 5/143 = NGMPP B25/15; Dimensions: 0.0 x 5.0 cm x 28 folios; Material: not specified; Condition: incomplete.
In the language of India: *Sthitisamuccaya*.
In the language of Tibet: *Gnas pa bsdus pa* (The Compendium of Abidings).
Homage to the Blessed One, the glorious Mañjuvajra!
Wooden covers with librarians' details;
second-hand manuscript cover page: *Kośakārikā*.
Oṃ. Homage to Mañjuśrī.
Having bowed to the selflessness of phenomena and persons, that [selflessness] is clearly taught here, following the sequence of the Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Vijñānavāda, and Madhyamaka. (1)
Vajra, you who possess the knowledge of fierce speech,
according to the stages of the Middle Way,
[realize] the selflessness of phenomena and persons, which is luminous clarity.
Now, the explanation of that very [Abhidharma] will be given.
The position of the Vaibhāṣikas is as follows:
Space and the two types of cessation—these three unconditioned phenomena are eternal.
And some maintain that the person (pudgala) is neither eternal nor non-eternal. (2)
Some assert that there is a "person" (pudgala),
saying it is neither permanent nor impermanent;
[they speak of] space and the two types of cessation.
The three unconditioned phenomena are permanent; all conditioned things are impermanent, and the world consists of the five aggregates.
That [world] should be known as the result, and it is the existence of the truth of suffering. (3)
"All conditioned things are impermanent;
the five aggregates that constitute the world are the truth of suffering."
Now, the fruit shall be explained: that which consists of afflictions and karma is the origin of causes and is to be abandoned;
both of these are truths with outflows (āsrava), while the two future [truths] are without outflows (anāsrava).
The cause is the truth of origination,
which consists of karma and the afflictions;
these two truths are contaminated.
The latter two are untainted (*anāsrava*). Cessation (*nirodha*), moreover, is the absolute exhaustion of afflictions and karma;
it is the liberation of the virtuous to be realized directly, the stilling and cessation of suffering. (5)
When [the afflictions] have been completely exhausted and have also been utterly ceased, they are to be directly realized.
The direct realization of the life of the Holy One is the peace that is the exhaustion of suffering; for that, one should cultivate the supreme Noble Eightfold Path which leads to liberation.
Right View... [6] ...That Noble Eightfold Path is the supreme means for certain deliverance through its cultivation.
Regarding the phrase "The Eightfold Path taught by the Sage," it is said: "The cultivation for the sake of the Śrāvaka and the Pratyekabuddha leads to Nirvāṇa."
But without instruction, [he arose] spontaneously from his previous vow.
This very [realization] is the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas,
and even the meditation of the pratyekabuddhas,
without depending upon prophecy.
Through his own previous aspirations, having directly realized the goal of nirvana with a remainder, he then performs a physical teaching by his own will and passes into final nirvana like a lamp. 8.
Having manifested the manifest body,
that Great Being passed into parinirvāṇa with a body possessing remainder.
Because he is capable of accomplishing the welfare of both himself and others, his greatness is absolute.
Therefore, his status is that of a "Middle Buddha"—such is the established position of the Vaibhāṣikas. (9)
Relying upon their own desires,
they attain parinirvāṇa like a lamp;
these are the Buddhas of the middling [capacity].
The Abiding of Proponents of Extremes: *Sūtrāntasthitiḥ*.
All conditioned phenomena—the aggregates, sense bases, and elements—are momentary.
The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements are momentary; once they have been made the object of correct knowledge, they are seen to be selfless and perish. 10.
The aggregates,
elements, and sense-fields—
all conditioned phenomena— are momentary.
On this day,
for me, [the object] has been made the domain of authentic cognition:
"Direct perception and inference are held to be the two types of valid cognition."
The object, however, is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), both by way of being indirect and by way of being direct. 11.
The manner of the two types of authentic cognition:
direct perception and inference,
[engage] with respect to the specific characteristics of their objects.
[The former] is manifest, [the latter] is hidden.
Because they share the same time and place, the momentary and the atom are capable of causal efficiency; therefore, only that is ultimately real. (12)
Because of its capacity; [the text reads] *maktatvāt* in the manuscript, emended to *śaktatvāt*.
Space and time are limited;
by means of subtle atoms and moments, they are restricted.
Because it is capable of performing its function,
that very thing is the ultimate reality;
by means of the exclusion of space and so forth, that alone is examined here.
As the object of valid cognition, [it is accepted] by all those who seek purposeful action.
Desiring all the purposes of activity for as long as space endures,
one takes [the object] as the domain of valid cognition.
This very point is thoroughly examined here:
for indeed, when a jar, a form, or the like performs a causal function at all times, it must perform it by its own nature alone; and that [nature] is distinct at every moment. (14)
"In this way,
forms such as a vase always perform their functional purpose;
even within each individual moment,"
It performs its own very nature;

for it does not perform that same purposeful action (arthakriyā) after having already performed it, because it is impossible to perform what has already been performed, nor does it perform another. || 15 ||
Having performed one action,
it is not that very same [action] which performs [it]; nor does the agent apply itself to the act of performing.
If [the thing] were produced, it would become something else; in every way, there would be no persistence of the previous form for even a single moment.
The nature of the preceding moment does not follow into any subsequent moment;
yet,
because moments appear as a continuous stream, [the illusion of continuity arises].
The various [cognitions] such as direct perception (*abhi-jñā*) abide separately; likewise,
they also definitively ascertain an object that has become presently manifest.
Now, this is the analytical discernment;
it is meditation arising from direct perception.
Once appearances have been thoroughly experienced,
It is not that another continuum is being posited; rather,
because one would fear the production of something else,
self-cognition would be impaired by its cause.
In the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, it is said:
"Regarding the body perceived as a coarse form,
[it is composed of] wood, earth, and so forth."
It is not that there is even a slight degree of attachment;
rather, pleasure and pain are distinct,
just as they are in the case of a jar and other such objects.
By moving one and making it red, all become moved and turn red; by causing one to tremble, [all likewise tremble].
It is likewise for that which pervades the entire body; yet,
if it is argued that [the whole] does not [move] because its parts move and so forth,
[that is not so].
If that which possesses parts does not move,
how could it reach another location?
[For] external objects are merely an aggregation of atoms.
Whatever momentary appearance there may be,
by the arising of the aspect of cognition itself,
the object itself is attained.
Omniscience is not attained through an object of experience that is merely [the nature] itself,
because it depends upon a single collection.
The cause is the equality of the faculties;
through the analysis of the half and the non-half,
the arising of distinctions in cognition is purposeless.
When analyzed through the categories of being, non-being, both,
and neither, there is no arising whatsoever;
even the four noble truths [are likewise].
"The wise should meditate upon this:
the perfectly complete bodhicitta does not exist unless the accumulations are complete."
One should not manifest [the realization]; if one does so, one will fall into the Lesser Vehicle...
[4 recto] ...gradually.
In the same way, for the Vaibhāṣika as well, [the result arises] from the application rooted in compassion. || 27 ||
Through familiarity with the stages of the profound [path],
compassion is the root of enlightenment;
by applying oneself thoroughly to the root of compassion;
It is likewise for those who speak with partiality: by practicing the stages of the Mahāyāna, who can prevent enlightenment?
Otherwise, how could this Mahāyāna—which is otherwise [than what you claim]—be [the word of the Buddha] for those who know the wisdom of the sūtras? (28)
By training in the stages of the Mahāyāna,
how could one not attain perfect enlightenment? Otherwise,
[what would be the point of] the realizations of those who follow the Sūtra vehicle?
How is it that the Blo de ji ltar theg chen yin (the Mahāyāna as it is) [is so]? Because without the Middle Way, even for them there is no Buddhahood.
Because vehicles exist merely as such, there is no certainty regarding their distinction. (29) [Since they are devoid of the Middle Way, there is no certainty.]
Even so, there is no Buddha;
because there is no fixed vehicle, due to the distinction of merely abiding [in suchness].
Arhatship through wisdom alone is seen in the Middle Way;
however, on the path [of the Bodhisattva], one is superior by means of giving and the other perfections due to the union of Mahāyāna compassion and wisdom. (30)
Wisdom alone is seen by the Arhats and even by the Madhyamikas;
[it is through] the Mahāyāna application of compassion [that one sees it fully].
The path of giving and so forth becomes superior;
the truths, such as suffering and the rest, also become otherwise through their different states.
If a distinction is intended based on the divisions of weak, medium, and so forth, [then the paths are likewise distinguished].
And when there is a distinction between those established in the vehicles, each is then ninefold;
[4v] for each,
the truths such as suffering and so forth—
The classification of the abodes changes;
if one thoroughly analyzes by distinguishing the categories of small, middling, and so forth,
[the distinctions become clear].
Now,
these nine distinct aspects are the classification of the abiding of the vehicle; this is the summary of the stability of the sūtras.
A Summary of the Abodes of the Sautrāntikas: *Nirākārayogācārasthitiḥ* (The Abode of the Aspectless Yogācāra)
Because atoms are partless, there is no mutual conjunction between them.
And if it were an entity in its entirety, there would never be any grossness.
Because it is devoid of even the slightest atomic part,
there is no mutual conjunction;
since all things are of a nature inseparable from it, [there is no such conjunction].
There is not even the slightest bit of color;
for those things that are beyond the senses and independent, even their collection is of the same nature.
If the property of cognition were grossness, how could it exist in the absence of an object? (33)
Even the gathering [of the elements] is likewise according to the Svātantrika school that transcends the senses;
if it were the meaning of coarse phenomena, [it would be otherwise].
And how could cognition be non-existent?
For it is not the case that this [cognition] is also a property of the object, because of the conceptual alternatives of difference and non-difference.
If it exists in subtle divisions, how could that same substance exist in gross divisions? (34)
Through thorough investigation of what has been divided and what has not been divided,
that ultimate phenomenon does not exist; yet,
it is divided by the analysis of subtle parts.
Just as it is with substances:

"Difference and non-difference cannot belong to a single thing because of contradiction, as can existence and non-existence. Furthermore, a single composite whole does not exist, due to such refutations as its being either one or many. (35)
Since existence and non-existence are contradictory,
there can be no identity between what is differentiated and what is undifferentiated;
for this would entail faults such as [the impossibility of] moving and not moving.
Not even a single [cognition] possesses parts;

for a restriction based on distinctions such as place and form does not establish the existence of an object, since such [restriction] occurs even in dreams, reflections, and the like, despite the absence of an object. (36)
Regarding the specific details such as direction and cloth,
there is no certainty concerning the object of accomplishment;
for this object is devoid of intrinsic reality.
"Just like a reflection in a mirror or the like," therefore, O Protector, blue and so forth, as well as consciousness, are not [established] by way of sublation.
First, a single [cognition] such as blue appears in a variegated form. (37)
Since blue and so forth have no objective reality,
consciousness is not tenable;
yet, because they appear in diverse forms, [consciousness exists].
Blue and so forth are not one and the same; nor is there consciousness [of them] when they are diverse, because they are not conjoined with one another.
Therefore, through the power of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), [consciousness appears] as if possessing the distinction between the grasped object and the grasping subject. (38)
Because they do not exist as mutually exclusive opposites,
consciousness is not manifold;
it is apprehended through the power of habitual tendencies.
"Because it is divided as if by grasping, the formless [consciousness] does not appear through distinctions such as blue and so forth;
and thus the Blessed One said: 'The world is representation-only. (39)
The various appearances, such as blue and so forth, are not real;
they are devoid of intrinsic nature due to delusion.
Thus, all beings are mere cognition.
Thus the Blessed One has said: "External objects do not exist in the way they are conceptualized by the foolish;
rather, the mind, stirred by habitual tendencies, manifests as the appearance of objects. (40)
Thus, because they have arisen in this way,
external objects as conceptualized do not exist;
it is the mind, stirred by habitual tendencies, [that appears].
Entering into the clear manifestation of the ultimate reality through the resolve that there is no mental aspect, because the triad is not perceived.
One should practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and vigor, each of which is threefold. || 41 ||
Through the conviction that they are formless,
the three are without an object of observation.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence—
these should be practiced with the three spheres rendered non-conceptual.
Having generated the wisdom consisting of hearing and reflection, one should cultivate that which consists of meditation.
One should rely upon the wisdom born of reflection and the wisdom born of cultivation through the yoga of meditative absorption, by means of calm abiding and insight. 42.
One should rely [on it];
through calm abiding (*śamatha*) and that which arises from reflection (*cintāmayī*).
Wisdom born from study, wisdom born from reflection, and through yoga born from meditative concentration,
there are calm abiding and special insight.
Thus it was said by the Blessed One:
"Having ascended to mind-only, one should not conceptualize external objects."
Having ascended to the external [object],
and abiding in the focal point of suchness (*tathatālambana*), one should transcend the mere-cognition (*citramātra*). 43.
Relying upon mind-only,
one does not investigate external objects.
Abiding in suchness,
one should also transcend sentient beings;
having transcended mind-only, one should transcend the appearance-less.
The yogin established in the non-manifestation beholds the Mahāyāna. 44. Having transcended mere mental construction, he sees.
One should transcend the absence of appearance;
the yogin who abides in the absence of appearance beholds the Mahāyāna.
The effortless state is peaceful, purified by aspirations; one perceives the supreme, selfless gnosis through non-appearance. (45) It is spontaneously accomplished and peaceful.
It is said: "Once one's aspirations have become completely pure,
one perceives the sublime primordial wisdom of selflessness,
which is without appearance."
Here, various forms conceptualized as suffering appear;
that supreme form of mantra arises from their latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Through the fulfillment of the path of generosity and so forth, there is cessation.
The perfected nature is the cessation [of conceptualization], formless, and mind-only. 46. Mind-only is the thorough investigation of that very manifestation, which is suffering.
The nature of the *kun ’byung* (origin) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) of habitual tendencies;
it is the cessation of the complete perfection of the path itself, such as generosity and so forth.
Its complete and perfect establishment is the non-existent mere-cognition (*vijñaptimātra*).
The summary of the position of the Nirākāra-Yogācāra.
The Summary of the Non-Conceptual Abode of the Path of Yogic Practice.
*Sākārayogācārasthitisamāsa*.
Whatever appears in any way whatsoever, that is cognition, most clearly manifest.
Just as in a dream, so too do these [objects] such as form appear. (47)
Whatever appearances arise, however many they may be, each of them is extremely clear within the mind;
just as it is so with the mind in a dream.

If forms and so forth appear individually, how indeed can there be a determination [of them] as mere appearances? If blue and the like were not consciousness, how else could they possess the nature of cognition? (48)
The mind that appears as various [objects] such as blue, is established within habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
If consciousness itself does not exist,
how could it be known through something else?
The Sage declared that superimposition, appearing as an object, occurs due to its outward-directed nature.
And because it is empty of the grasped and the grasper, he therefore declared it to be without appearance (nirābhāsa). 49.
The Muni spoke thus:
"When grasping and the grasper are empty, that which is without appearance is asserted as purity."
Therefore, blue and so forth are not external objects,
because they appear within consciousness.

Therefore, one who is free from conceptual construction and possesses great compassion should meditate in all its aspects. (50) Since consciousness appears as [objects], there are no objects such as blue and so forth.
"Therefore, everyone should cultivate the aspects;

non-conceptuality and great compassion are [the essence]. Having destroyed the accumulation known as latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) through the path of generosity and so forth, [one attains the result].
One attains the cessation of all sufferings, which is manifold yet non-dual. || 51 ||
Regarding the teaching on the latencies of co-emergence:
abandon the latencies of generosity and so forth;
this is also the cessation of all suffering.

Seeing that the two—the collection of phenomena and so forth—are non-dual, one makes the Dharmakāya, which is the emptiness of subject and object endowed with the excellence of all aspects, manifest; then the Sambhogakāya radiates forth as a mass of light. 52.
From the dharmakāya that clarifies the emptiness of subject and object, endowed with the supreme of all aspects,

Through the power of appearance, it is not non-existent, because of the existence of the apprehended object and so forth; likewise, it is neither both, nor is it another form, due to the lack of realization. 53.
The entity that is devoid of grasping and so forth does not exist as the habitual tendency for appearances;
likewise, both do not exist.
One does not conceive of [the object] as other than its form; thus, being free from the four extremes, it is not devoid of intrinsic nature.
For non-conceptual gnosis, however, has intrinsic nature because of its self-cognition within itself. (54)
This entity, which is liberated from the four extremes,
is not non-existent;
yet its nature is non-conceptual.
"Primordial wisdom is self-knowing direct experience"—this is the summary of the position of the Yogācāra school with aspects (*sākāravijñānavāda*). o ||
This is the summary of the stages of the Yogācāra practitioner, including the various types of activities.
*Madhyamāsthiti* (The Middle Abiding).
The refutation of non-existence by the three— by the vulgar, by the non-Buddhists,
and by the Buddhists.
It is well-adorned; however, the imputation of existence upon phenomena is indeed a fault.
"The Buddha was not included within my lineage;
since the three [times] are not asserted to be non-existent,
the sublime Dharma is excellent and beautiful."
Abiding in the middle way is the absence of sin; it is free from all superimpositions.
Having prostrated, the reasoning and scripture for the removal of superimposition are now set forth. (56)
The very nature of the Great Middle Way,
which completely abandons all abidings,
is the exhaustion of abiding through prostration.
It shall be explained through scripture and reasoning:
Those very elements that are established as being dependently arisen and momentary are likewise devoid of intrinsic nature, because they lack both unity and plurality. (57)
Whatever is established from the elements themselves,
arising from conditions and momentary,
is devoid of being one or many.
That very [body] is non-existent as a single entity, because it is divided into the thighs, eyes, head, back, and so forth.
It is not one, for the arms and other parts likewise possess internal divisions in each of their respective portions. (58)
When this body is divided into its parts—
the limbs, the head, the back,
and so forth— not even a single part, such as a hand, remains.
Thus, it arises from being divided into parts; even down to the atom, that [atom] has been analyzed.
By means of the body alone, those things such as the mountains and the earth are known. 59.
By means of the body itself,
having divided that very existence,
one analyzes it down to its subtle particles.
Regarding the body itself, as explained [in the treatise],
it is known as the support and the supported and so forth; because its nature is a single integration, multiplicity does not exist therein.
And thus there would be no sublation of what precedes, since [all things] are established as being equal to a dream.
Since a single entity is negated,
even the manifold does not exist;
it is equal to a dream and to meditative equipoise.
Nor is it tenable that there is no contradiction because [the object] has the nature of cognition,
for the wise consider the presentation of the form to be by way of generality (sāmānyena). 61.
Because the nature of cognition lacks intrinsic existence, it does not contradict awareness itself; for this reason,
by means of a general logical argument, [it is established].
This is the method of the sublime expression:
"This entire universe is devoid of intrinsic nature, yet it performs purposeful activity through its functional operation."
Since both knowledge and the object of knowledge are [unreal], what is the use of our investigation? (62)
This manifold [world], which has the capacity to perform functions conventionally,
does not exist [ultimately] like a corpse;
it is merely cognition and the object of cognition.
"O friend, what is it that is being thoroughly examined?
It is consciousness itself, because it appears here as form and so forth.
Thus, O wise ones, the lack of proof for this means of establishment is not to be entertained. (63)
The appearance of forms and so forth as distinct entities is,
for consciousness itself,
like a ritual procedure (sādhana).
For one who is not defeated by the reasoning of the wise, that which arises conventionally has no arising in reality;
therefore, because it is unarisen, the mind is by its very nature devoid of intrinsic existence. 64.
Conventionally, there is arising,
yet that is the meaning of non-arising; therefore,
the mind is non-arisen.
Because there is no intrinsic nature, it is so.
For the birth of an existent is not established because it already exists;
nor is the birth of a non-existent established from itself because it does not exist.
Nor does there arise from another in an intrinsic nature, because of the absence of a cause. (65)
Existence is established through the accomplishment of arising;
because it exists, non-existence also does not exist.
Since the entity of a cause does not exist, [the effect does not exist].
Not produced from another by way of its own nature, its form is neither real nor false, like a reflection in a mirror;
in that very same way, the wise understand the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. (66)
Just as a reflected image appears,
it is neither true nor false;
such is the nature of all phenomena.
In the system of those who know the intrinsic nature, the conventional existence of things such as houses and clothes is a mere designation based on a collection;
that [designation] applies to the collection itself as well. Thus, all is peace, because there is no arising. (67)
"Things such as houses, clothes, and so forth, which are fabricated,
are conventional entities;
since these have no intrinsic nature, they are unarisen."
The same is true for the state of being deluded.
For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "This world is a mere name;
indeed, all these [concepts] have been proclaimed by me as things that flow toward others. (68)
Therefore, the Blessed One himself said:
"These wandering beings are merely names;
all these things spoken of by others [are likewise]."
"I have spoken correctly; having first uttered the Yakṣa, their [wrong] understanding is averted. Having averted their understanding here, I shall teach my own position. (69)
The directions were mentioned previously;
this is the analysis of the intellect.
Having cleared away that intellect, [one proceeds].
I shall explain my own position:
just as the universe appears in mirrors, it is devoid of both identity and difference.
And yet it is not found there; likewise is the nature of things among all phenomena.
Just as a reflection in a mirror is devoid of being either one with or other than [the original], so too is the horse.
There is nothing that exists apart from appearance; such is the nature of things. The world is like an illusion or a dream, devoid of causes and conditions.
For whom there is always no cause, and no conceptual constructions arise. || 71 ||
The world is like an illusion or a dream; it is utterly devoid of causes and conditions, yet appears perpetually and without interruption.
Conceptualization does not arise; where no objective entity exists, there is only mind.
How can mind be without an object? It is not tenable that there is "mind-only. (72)
Since no entity exists therein,
one should realize it as mind-only;
for how could there be a mind that lacks an entity?
It is not logical for it to be Mind-Only;
for if the mind functions through the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender, this is indeed a worldly mind, and "Mind-Only" is not tenable. (73)
If the mind engages through the distinction between grasper and grasped,
these minds of the worldly realm [arise].
It is not logical that [the world] be mind-only.
For if it were to arise like a dream, appearing as the body, enjoyments, and the environment, it would follow that there are two minds; yet a single mind does not possess two characteristics. (74)
If the body, enjoyments,
and sense faculties arise like a dream,
then the mind would become twofold.
The nature of the mind is non-dual.
For just as a sword cannot cut its own blade, and just as a fingertip cannot touch itself, so too the mind [cannot perceive itself]. (75)
Because it cannot be cut by the edge of a sword,
nor can it be touched by one's own fingertips.
In the same way, the nature of mind is its own manifestation;
through a mind that appears like a reflected image,
by means of an intellect previously cultivated through training, [one realizes it].
Seeing how things arise,
one perceives that the aspects of objects are not real; [one sees] the person,
the causes, and the aggregates.
The conditions of similarity, atoms,
a primary creator such as Īśvara,
and mind-only are thoroughly analyzed.
To perceive external objects is an error; there are no objects other than the mind itself.
Having analyzed this with reasoning, one examines it within the mind.
It is the cessation of subject and object;
when analyzed by the intellect,
its intrinsic nature is certainly ungraspable.
Because it is now inexpressible, it is shown to be without substantial entity;
when the mind conceptualizes it with the intellect, [it is seen as such].
If there is no dependent nature and no imagined nature,
and if the thoroughly established nature does not exist,
how could the mind perform analysis?
Without intrinsic nature and without a cognizer,
there is no non-existent basis either;
because its capacity is like that of a reflection.
These are conceptualized by the evil imagination;
they are cognitions of entities and characteristics.
From whatever mental fluctuation and instability there is, [arise these].
When my bodies have passed away,
I shall conduct myself with non-conceptuality;
suchness and emptiness are the limit.
Nirvana and the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu),
as well as all phenomena that are unborn,
are the nature of the ultimate truth.
External entities and non-entities are not grasped at all by the mind;
that which has abandoned all views—
It has the characteristic of non-arising;
for when the conditions for an assemblage exist,
there occurs both engagement and cessation.
When the collection has become separate,
there is neither arising nor ceasing...
... conceptual proliferation does not proceed; it ceases. || 86 ||
Neither existent nor non-existent, there is no arising of things; the mind is neither existent nor non-existent,
because it arises from the gathering of other factors.
"When this entire world is seen as nothing but a mental construction, and there is neither engagement nor withdrawal, then the mind becomes concentrated in meditative absorption. (87)
When one sees that all these worlds are merely aggregations,
this very collection is nothing more than a mere assemblage.
At that time, the mind abides in equanimity;
for him nothing arises, and nothing is obstructed. What is it that is not obstructed for him?

the supreme Mahāmudrā;
yet those who do not possess knowledge of the reality of phenomena (dharmatattva) have not exerted themselves [in this].
For the sake of entering into the true nature of reality (dharmatattva), their distinction has been demonstrated. || 170 ||
As has been shown:
"One who knows the true nature of phenomena does not undergo suffering."
Because he abides in the suchness of phenomena (dharmatā),
he is shown to be the one who acts;
through the instruction of the true guru, it becomes clear, and not otherwise.
Even when urged by a black [horse], this person does not understand the meaning from it. || 171 ||
Even when prompted by another,
this [realization] becomes clear through the oral instructions of the Venerable Guru,
and not otherwise.
"By another's instruction, the meaning is not realized here; *dharmodaya* is gnosis, gnosis... [the rest is lost].
The wisdom born from the arising of phenomena is said to be the realization of this just as it is;
through one's own inclination, the meaning of the words [is realized].
The apprehended object is not real;
likewise, all four [objects] are also [unreal].
That which is spoken of as "beginning with this" is...
Just as that is the fourth body (nirmāṇakāya),
it is clarified through the skillful means of the sublime guru;
emptiness is the very nature of bliss.
Desiring great bliss, bliss,
and supreme bliss, bliss itself with equal taste,
the coemergent dharmakāya.
Because that very [nature] brings about the welfare of bliss,
it is the enjoyment body and the emanation body as well;
it is the very essence of the fivefold flavor.
"All are primordial and without distinction," and "The nature of the five bodies of the Buddha."
Although it is said in such passages as these,
the attainment of the five bodies is by way of their being of one taste in reality.
The four *skus* are differentiated,
yet because they are non-dual, there is the fifth;
this very oneness is suchness itself.
Such is the nature of the *sukha* (bliss) as it is asserted;
just as this is engaged in by my own mind through individual cognition (*pratisaṃvedana*) and meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*).
Just as the wisdom of the sublime Dharma has attained realization within the land through its intelligence,
this has been expressed here in brief.
May all beings become vessels for realizing the meaning of how things arise.
This concludes the *Compendium of Abidings*.

"Translated from the presence of the great master Śrī Sahajavajra and the Indian preceptor Dhariśrījñāna by the Tibetan translator Rma ban Chos ’bar. Later, it was requested by Par ston and finalized by comparing the original manuscript with the Indian preceptor and the translator of Mchur."

The *Compendium of Abiding* is complete. It was composed by the great master, the glorious Sahajavajra, and translated by the Indian preceptor Dhariśrījñāna and the Tibetan translator Rma ban Chos ’bar. Later, it was revised by Bar ston and finalized by comparing it with the original manuscript through the Indian preceptor and Mtshur lo tsā ba.
